newsitem.title: JAPAN: Takefuji says offer to ex-MOF official not wrong.
newsitem.headline: Takefuji says offer to ex-MOF official not wrong.

text.p: Takefuji Corp said on Friday it had offered 19,000 of its shares to a retired Finance Ministry official in March 1994 before the shares were listed on the OTC market, but did not believe it was wrong to do so.
Several major Japanese newspapers reported on Friday that the former ministry official acquired Takefuji stock in the name of his daughter, whose husband is currently employed by the ministry.
The reports rattled investors, sending shares in the consumer finance firm lower. Finance Minister Wataru Kubo described the matter as very regrettable.
The retired ministry official, who left his post nearly 20 years ago, was working as a part-time auditor for Takefuji at the time he was offered the shares.
A Takefuji spokesman confirmed that the company had offered shares to the retired ministry official before the over-the-counter listing, but said there was no legal problem with doing so.
The company said in a statement: "We asked Mr Hiromi Tokuda, our part-time auditor, to have our shares as we sought stable shareholders. And we understand that there is no legal problem with that."

Tokuda, a former director-general of the ministry's banking bureau, proposed that his daughter buy the shares instead, saying he was too old, a Takefuji spokesman said. The daughter then acquired the shares, the spokesman said.

"Mr Tokuda was worried that he could get profits from the purchase and so, we think, he sold the shares voluntarily (through his daughter) before the listing of shares," the statement said. His daughter's husband is a serving MOF official, the company said.
Finance Minister Kubo said in a news conference on Friday morning that the reported involvement of a former MOF official in the purchase of shares in another person's name was very regrettable.
Tokuda resigned from his job as adviser to Nomura Research Institute Ltd on Friday, Nomura Research said in a statement without providing reasons for his resignation.

The Takefuji spokesman said Tokuda's daughter bought the shares after receiving a loan of 24.5 million yen from a finance firm. In July this year, the shares were sold, the spokesman said, adding that Takefuji did not know until then that Tokuda's son-in-law was a Finance Ministry employee.
Tokuda could not be contacted for comment on the matter.

The Takefuji spokesman said the share transactions did not breach the law. He also said the shares were sold before the firm was registered on the OTC market in August this year, and the family did not make any profits from the transactions.
The Ministry of of Finance (MOF) said in a statement that Tokuda's son-in-law, who works for the ministry, was not involved in the matter. "The MOF official had no link with the incident," it said.
Although Tokuda left the ministry many years ago, he is a member of the financial system council, an advisory panel to the finance minister.
The ministry has come under attack in recent years for its close links to the financial industry.
